content.p: Gabby Petito was 22 when she and her fiancé, Brian Laundrie, 23, set out in a converted white Ford Transit van to see the American West and film it for social media. On 1 September 2021 Laundrie arrived at his parents' home in North Port, Florida, driving the van without her. Her family reported her missing on 11 September, and on 19 September her body was found near a remote campsite on the edge of Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming. A coroner ruled that she had been strangled.

Laundrie never faced a court over her death. He vanished into a Florida nature reserve on 13 September, and his remains were found there on 20 October. In January 2022 the FBI said a notebook found beside them contained written statements in which he claimed responsibility for her death. That statement is his own claim, relayed by the FBI; it was never tested in a trial. The years since have been taken up by lawsuits against his estate, his parents and the Moab police, one of which went on appeal to the Utah Supreme Court.
content.h2: A trip that began on the road from New York
content.p: Petito and Laundrie grew up on Long Island and had been living with his parents in North Port for more than a year when they set out. According to ABC News, North Port's police chief said they planned to drive west in her van to visit state and national parks. They left from Blue Point, New York, in early July, and posted as Nomadic Statik on YouTube and Instagram. Petito's Instagram showed Great Sand Dunes National Park in Colorado on 10 July.

The online picture was sunny. The record that came out later was not. A 911 recording and police body-camera footage released during the search suggested, in the words of Global News, "a darker side" to the relationship.

On 12 August a caller told a 911 dispatcher that he had driven past a couple outside the Moonflower Community Cooperative in Moab, Utah. "The gentleman was slapping the girl," he said, and the two "ran up and down the sidewalk" before the man "proceeded to hit her" and drove off. Officers found the white van, which the report says Laundrie was driving, and pulled it over on the road toward Arches National Park after it crossed a double yellow line and hit a curb.

On the body-camera footage Petito is crying as she describes an argument that escalated. She told officers that she had slapped Laundrie and hit him first, and that Laundrie had grabbed her face. KUTV reported that Laundrie told officers Petito had left visible scratches on his face. One officer wrote that it appeared to be a mental or emotional health "break" rather than a domestic assault, and KUTV reported that the officers decided they were dealing with a "mental health crisis." No one was charged. They told the couple to spend the night apart; Petito kept the van and police took Laundrie to a motel, the independent review later said. Moab's police chief, Bret Edge, said at the time that "insufficient evidence existed to justify criminal charges."

Petito's mother, Nichole Schmidt, told ABC News she last spoke to her daughter by phone on 25 August, when Petito said they had stopped at Grand Teton on the way to Yellowstone. That day's Instagram post was the last on her account. Florida police said in a search-warrant affidavit, as CNN reported, that Schmidt received an odd text on 27 August, which the affidavit described as the last communication from her.

Two witnesses later spoke publicly. Nina Angelo told CNN she saw a "commotion" as Petito and Laundrie left The Merry Piglets restaurant in Jackson, Wyoming, on 27 August, with Petito in tears and Laundrie visibly angry; she did not see any violence. Miranda Baker said in TikTok videos that she and her boyfriend gave Laundrie a ride on 29 August in Wyoming. Baker said he told them he had been camping alone for days while Petito worked on social media from the van. The FBI had not confirmed her account when ABC News reported it.

The FBI asked for information from anyone who used the Spread Creek Dispersed Camping Area between 27 and 30 August. In the depositions that Laundrie's parents gave in a later lawsuit, they said their son phoned them on 29 August and repeatedly said "Gabby's gone", without ever saying he had killed her, according to his father, who said he did not think at the time that his son had done so. Laundrie asked for help finding a lawyer, they said, and arrived home on 1 September.

Petito's family reported her missing to the Suffolk County Police Department in New York. "Two people went on a trip, one person returned, and that person isn't cooperating," North Port's police chief, Todd Garrison, said at a press conference. The Laundrie family's attorney, Steven Bertolino, said the family would stay silent on legal advice. On 14 September a statement from that attorney expressed the family's hope that Petito would be "reunited with her family."

Searchers found Petito's remains on Sunday 19 September. Teton County Coroner Dr. Brent Blue classified the death as a homicide but did not disclose how she was killed. On 12 October he announced that she was strangled and had died three to four weeks before she was found. The Associated Press noted that this put her death around 27 to 30 August, the period when investigators believed the couple was in that area. Blue declined to say more, citing Wyoming law limiting what coroners can release. The Associated Press later quoted a coroner's determination of "blunt-force injuries to the head and neck, with manual strangulation."

Laundrie left the family home in a Ford Mustang on 13 September, telling his parents he was going to hike in the Carlton Reserve, a swampy reserve of about 25,000 acres near North Port. His parents reported him missing on 17 September. North Port police later admitted they had mistaken Roberta Laundrie, driving the Mustang back on 15 September, for her son; a police spokesman said that "it likely changed nothing" and that there was a "very good possibility that Brian was already deceased."

On 22 September a federal arrest warrant was issued, and the following day the FBI announced that a grand jury in the US District Court in Wyoming had indicted Laundrie over a Capital One bank card and someone's personal identification number, alleging unauthorized withdrawals or charges above $1,000 between about 30 August and 1 September. The indictment did not say whose card it was. Bertolino said his understanding was that the warrant concerned activity after Petito's death, not the death itself. The FBI said the warrant would let officers pursue Laundrie anywhere while the homicide inquiry went on. Searchers waded through water that was in places waist-deep.

On 20 October, Laundrie's parents joined a search of the reserve that began on the day it reopened to the public, with law enforcement accompanying them. Christopher Laundrie picked up a dry bag, and officers then found a backpack and, nearby, skeletal remains. FBI special agent in charge Michael McPherson said the items, including a notebook, were in an area that had until recently been underwater. On 21 October the FBI said a comparison of dental records confirmed the remains were Laundrie's. The family's attorney said the first autopsy was inconclusive and sent the remains to an anthropologist.

On 21 January 2022 the FBI's Denver office announced that its investigation was over. "All logical investigative steps have been concluded in this case," said special agent in charge Michael Schneider. "The investigation did not identify any other individuals other than Brian Laundrie directly involved in the tragic death of Gabby Petito."

The FBI said a review of the notebook "revealed written statements by Mr. Laundrie claiming responsibility for Ms. Petito's death." It did not say what the notebook contained, according to the Associated Press. The FBI also said text messages had passed between Laundrie's phone and Petito's after her death, and that "the timing and content of these messages are indicative of Mr. Laundrie attempting to deceive law enforcement by giving the impression that Ms. Petito was still alive." A medical examiner in Florida ruled that he died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound; a revolver was recovered with the other items. The statement from Petito's family said the FBI's facts "leave no doubt the Brian Laundrie murdered Gabby." Laundrie's family lawyer said the closure might let each family "begin to heal."
content.h2: What Moab's police were found to have done wrong
content.p: The city of Moab said in September 2021 that it knew of no breach of police policy, but would commission a formal investigation; the police chief, Edge, went on medical leave later that month. The review was done by Captain Brandon Ratcliffe of the Price City Police Department, and Moab released its 102 pages on 12 January 2022.

Ratcliffe concluded that the officers, Eric Pratt and Daniel Scott Robbins, had made "several unintentional mistakes." The incident should have been classified as domestic violence, which under Utah law would have required an arrest or a citation, and on the facts then available that would have been against Petito. Because it was recorded as disorderly conduct, no report went to prosecutors. The officers' reports did not document any injury to her, and the review found that no one appeared to ask Laundrie about a scratch on her neck. No statement was taken from the 911 caller. He recommended probation for both officers and more training in domestic-violence cases and report writing; one officer, Robbins, was in the final phase of field training.

Ratcliffe also wrote that "it's very likely Gabby was a long-term victim of domestic violence," even if she was the main aggressor in that one incident. On whether she would be alive if police had acted differently, he wrote: "Nobody knows." The city said the officers made unintentional mistakes and that it believed they acted with respect and empathy.

Against Laundrie's estate. In May 2022 Petito's mother sued his estate for wrongful death, seeking damages above $30,000. In November 2022 a Sarasota County circuit judge entered a final judgment of $3 million. FOX 13 described it as a judgment; ABC7 used the word "settled". The family's lawyer, Patrick Reilly, called the sum arbitrary and said Laundrie's estate was "very minimal." Any money would go to the Gabby Petito Foundation.

Against Laundrie's parents and their lawyer. Petito's parents, Joseph Petito and Nichole Schmidt, sued Christopher and Roberta Laundrie and Bertolino for intentional infliction of emotional distress, alleging that they knew she was dead while the family sought her. In June 2022 Judge Hunter Carroll refused to dismiss the claim against the Laundries. In February 2024 CNN reported on the depositions. Roberta Laundrie said a "burn after reading" letter found in her son's backpack was a "jokey, stupid letter" written before the trip. The case was resolved after mediation, reported in February 2024; Bertolino said the terms were confidential, and the Petitos said the parties agreed "in order to avoid further legal expenses and prolonged personal conflict."

Against the Moab police. In November 2022 the family filed a $50 million wrongful death suit, alleging negligence by the department and its officers. The city denied responsibility. On 20 November 2024 Judge Don Torgerson of Utah's 7th District Court dismissed it, saying he had to follow current law on governmental immunity but that a higher court could consider whether that law is constitutional. The family appealed to the Utah Supreme Court, asking it to overturn the 1996 precedent Tiede v. State. KSL reported in January 2026 that oral argument was set for 4 March 2026 and that Utah had filed a brief supporting Moab. No decision on the appeal has been reported.
